meta.title: Earth candidate analog site catalog
meta.description: Globally curated candidate terrestrial analog environments for Moon/Mars exploration. Climate features are fetched from NASA POWER (see scripts/fetch_power.mjs); geology/terrain tags and notes are curated from published analog literature and geological maps. Coordinates point at the representative study area, not an administrative center.

tag_definitions.volcanic_basalt: Basaltic/mafic volcanic terrain (lava plains, shields, fissures)
tag_definitions.impact_crater: Meteorite impact structure (young, exposed, or eroded)
tag_definitions.aeolian_dunes: Active dune fields / wind-shaped landforms (yardangs included)
tag_definitions.salt_flat: Evaporite playa, salt pan, sulfate/chloride crusts
tag_definitions.permafrost_ice: Continuous permafrost, ground ice, patterned ground
tag_definitions.subsurface_cave: Caves, lava tubes, karst — subsurface environments
tag_definitions.fluvial_paleolake: Ancient lake beds, deltas, channels, badland drainage

meta.barrenness_scale: 0 = densely vegetated, 1 = abiotic surface with no vegetation
meta.relief_m: Approximate local relief within the study area (curated from DEM-based literature)

notes.why: The driest soil environment measured on Earth — parts of the core may not have seen measurable rain for decades to centuries. Soils contain Mars-relevant perchlorates and show organic depletion nearly as severe as martian regolith, making it the benchmark for Mars soil-dry-limit studies.
notes.breakdown: Atmosphere, gravity and radiation remain fully terrestrial; daytime temperatures are mild compared with Mars.
notes.studies: Navarro-Gonzalez et al. 2003/2006 (Science, Mars-like Atacama soils); NASA ASTEP/Atacama Rover Astrobiology Drilling Studies (ARADS).

notes.why: Peruvian counterpart of the Atacama core with some of the most sterile soils on Earth; used by NASA Ames to test life-detection instruments against the driest Earth baseline.
notes.breakdown: Warm days, Earth-level atmospheric pressure and oxygen; no martian-style dust storms.
notes.studies: McKay et al. NASA Ames Atacama instrument field tests; Catling et al. 2018 (dry-limit astrobiology).

notes.why: High-altitude (4.3 km) geyser field with intense UV, freezing nights, silica sinter terraces and near-constant dust devils — a Mars analog for hydrothermal alteration under high irradiance and a rover/sensor calibration site.
notes.breakdown: Liquid water is abundant; atmospheric pressure still ~60% of sea level, far above Mars.
notes.studies: NASA/SETI Institute El Tatio Mars analog campaigns; Boston et al. silica biosignature studies.

sites.name: Puna de Atacama salars (Antofagasta de la Sierra)

notes.why: High-altitude volcanic plateau (>3.5 km) with salars, evaporites and volcanic fields; strong UV flux and low humidity approximate early-Mars surface chemistry conditions.
notes.breakdown: Substantially colder nights than Earth lowlands but still milder than Mars; water persists in salars.
notes.studies: Puna evaporite Mars-analog studies (e.g., Salar de Antofalla halophile research).

notes.why: The world's largest salt flat (10,000+ km²) — polygonal evaporite crusts and halite megapolygons on a high plateau, directly comparable to martian chloride/sulfate-bearing terrains seen from orbit.
notes.breakdown: Wet season flooding and Earth-normal atmosphere; halite rather than the sulfates common on Mars.
notes.studies: Evaporite polygon analog studies for Mars chloride deposits (e.g., Osterloo et al. follow-ups).

notes.why: One of the hottest, most acidic places on Earth: hydrothermal acid-sulfate brines, iron oxide terraces and massive salt domes below sea level — a direct analog for Mars Meridiani-type acid-sulfate alteration and for the habitability edge of life.
notes.breakdown: Extreme heat is Earth-driven (solar + geothermal), not martian; gravity and pressure are terrestrial.
notes.studies: López-García et al. / Cavicchioli halophile surveys; 2019 'geomicrobiology of Dallol' (PNAS-related) studies of the sterile hyper-acidic ponds.

notes.why: Active basaltic shield volcano with a persistent lava lake in a desert rift — living analog for basaltic effusive volcanism that built the martian Tharsis shields and lunar maria.
notes.breakdown: Eruption temperatures/degassing are far more vigorous than present-day Mars.
notes.studies: Afar rift volcanology; thermal remote-sensing calibration studies for planetary lava flows.

notes.why: Africa's lowest point (-155 m), among its hottest and most hyperarid spots, ringed by basalt and evaporating into hypersaline brine — evaporite deposition in a desert rift basin, analogous to closed-basin lakes on Mars.
notes.breakdown: Standing hypersaline water is present; Mars analogs concern the salt record, not the water.
notes.studies: Danakil evaporite geochemistry studies; Mars closed-basin chloride analog work.

notes.why: Hottest land surface temperature ever measured by satellite (MODIS ~70.7 °C) on a dark lava/gypsum plateau, flanked by the world's tallest yardangs (the Kaluts) — an analog for martian equatorial thermal maxima and wind-carved yardang provinces like Medusae Fossae.
notes.breakdown: Air temperature remains far below surface value; Earth's winds are stronger than Mars's thin-air gusts.
notes.studies: MODIS Land Surface Temperature record (Mildrexler et al.); yardang morphometry comparisons with Mars.

notes.why: The single largest dust source on Earth: winds funneling through the Tibesti mountains lift diatomite flakes from a former lake bed — the best terrestrial process analog for dust lifting that feeds martian dust storms, and for dusty paleolake basins.
notes.breakdown: Dust is lifted into a dense humid atmosphere; Mars dust events are driven by thin-air dynamics and thermal tides.
notes.studies: Bodélé dust emission studies (Koren, Todd, Washington); Mars global dust storm dust-source literature.

notes.why: The oldest desert on Earth (~55 Myr) with a full dune-type inventory: star dunes to 380 m, linear dunes, barchans and interdune pans — the reference dune-field analog for Mars dune morphology and fog-adapted life in hyperarid terrain.
notes.breakdown: Fog delivers moisture; Mars dunes are formed/modified under far lower air density.
notes.studies: Livingstone & Bristow Namib dune dynamics; fog-water harvesting biology (Stenocarpa/Namib lichens).

notes.why: A 5,000 km² dry lakebed playa — seasonal desiccation polygons, dust-lifting surface and sedimentary layering analogous to martian paleolake floors (e.g., Jezero's playa facies).
notes.breakdown: Seasonal water and biology remain; Mars analog concerns the desiccated state.
notes.studies: Etosha playa sedimentology; Mars playa/paleolake comparative studies.

notes.why: A 2.5 km, ~5 Ma impact crater partly buried by migrating dunes — a natural laboratory for impact-landform degradation by wind, exactly the process that reshapes old craters on Mars.
notes.breakdown: Simple-crater scale only; no ejecta-plain complexity like large lunar basins.
notes.studies: Roter Kamm geology and dune-impact interaction studies (Miller & Smit).

notes.why: One of Earth's largest salt-pans complexes — remnant of a paleo-megalake with polygonal salt crusts, an analog for martian closed-basin evaporites and paleolake sedimentology.
notes.breakdown: Annual inundation and microbial mats; Mars analog is the desiccated end-state.
notes.studies: Paleo-Lake Makgadikgadi reconstructions; salt-crust polygon analog studies.

notes.why: A young (~21 ka), 1.9 km simple crater excavated in hard granitic/gneissic basement with a crisp rim and ejecta — a small fresh-crater analog resembling kilometer-scale lunar and martian craters.
notes.breakdown: Scale (km vs tens of km on the Moon) and absence of shock-melt sheet exposure at lunar scale.
notes.studies: Tenoumer impactite studies; simple-crater morphometry comparisons.

notes.why: A well-preserved (~300 ka) 880 m simple crater rising from a dune field — impact morphology interacting with aeolian sediments, similar to crater-dune interplay seen in Mars craters.
notes.breakdown: Small size; weathered cone deposits differ from pristine lunar rims.
notes.studies: Wolfe Creek geophysics/impactite studies; dune-crater interaction literature.

notes.why: A 142 Ma, 22 km complex impact structure preserved as a 5 km annular ring of breccia — the eroded-inner-ring analog for heavily degraded complex craters on Mars and ancient lunar terrains.
notes.breakdown: Deep erosion removes the original crater form; vegetation encroaches on flanks.
notes.studies: Gosses Bluff impactite/shock studies; degraded-crater morphometry analog work.

notes.why: A hyperarid limestone shelf with hundreds of known karst caves and collapse dolines plus a dense concentration of meteorite finds (Mundrabilla) — an analog for subsurface exploration techniques and meteorite accumulation surfaces.
notes.breakdown: Karst chemistry (carbonic-acid dissolution) has no lunar/martian equivalent; caves are limestone, not basalt.
notes.studies: Nullarbor meteorite programs; cave-analog work on planetary lava-tube exploration robotics.

notes.why: Classic 150 m barchanoid dune field with seasonal sand-transport reversals — a compact analog for Mars barchan dune fields and for testing mobility/traction in loose granular terrain.
notes.breakdown: Earth gravity and wind density; Mars dunes migrate slower under thinner air.
notes.studies: Erg Chebbi dune morphometry; Mars barchan analog comparisons (Bourke et al.).

notes.why: Europe's only true desert, dissected into gullied badlands with episodic flash floods — a fluvial-erosion analog for martian gullies and channel incision under episodic water.
notes.breakdown: Rainfall is orders of magnitude above Mars; erosion rates much faster.
notes.studies: Mars gully analog studies in Tabernas; ESA rover mobility trials in badland terrain.

notes.why: A 7 km basaltic lava tube descending into the ocean — ESA PANGAEA's astronaut geology classroom and the reference analog for martian/lunar lava-tube skylights and underground shelters.
notes.breakdown: Tube formation rates and magma chemistry differ from mare basalt; Earth geothermal gradients are higher.
notes.studies: ESA PANGAEA-X campaigns; lunar/martian lava tube skylight literature (Haruyama et al., Cushing et al.).

notes.why: The world's largest 'makhtesh' — a 40 km erosion crater that LOOKS like an impact basin but was carved by fluvial denudation of a domed anticline. A deliberate teaching case: visual similarity alone misleads, which is why this catalog scores process, not appearance.
notes.breakdown: Genetically unrelated to impacts — useful to show why multi-dataset analogs beat eye-candy.
notes.studies: Negev desert research; Israel Space Agency Mars-analog field trials in Ramon.

notes.why: Iron-oxide-stained sandstone/granite valley system with dunes, inselbergs and canyons — the operational analog used for Mars rover-field-trial planning and astronaut terrain-recognition training.
notes.breakdown: Sandstone and granite lithologies differ from basaltic Mars crust.
notes.studies: Mars analog terrain perception studies; multiple film/mission rehearsal deployments.

notes.why: A 20,000 km² basaltic lava field with ~500 scoria cones and extensive pāhoehoe/ʻaʻā flows — a young, vast mare-style basalt plain analog used for Mars-mission field exercises.
notes.breakdown: Recent activity (1256 CE) means heat/gas sources absent on today's Moon.
notes.studies: Saudi Geological Survey Mars-analog field campaigns (2018-2022).

notes.why: A 2.3 km diameter, 250 m deep volcanic maar floored by white salt crust inside a basaltic harrat — small-crater morphology plus evaporite floor in one site (again: volcanic, NOT impact — another visual-vs-process lesson).
notes.breakdown: Explosion mechanism is phreatomagmatic, unrelated to impact processes.
notes.studies: Al Wahbah crater geology studies; maar analog comparisons.

notes.why: A young (<300 yr) ~116 m impact crater chain excavated INTO loose eolian sand — the direct analog for small craters forming in unconsolidated regolith, like fresh lunar secondary craters.
notes.breakdown: Tiny scale; impact glass/iron fragments unique to Earth's oxygen-rich surface.
notes.studies: Wabar crater surveys (Philby, Shoemaker-era revisits).

notes.why: A hyperarid 2.8 km-altitude basin with Mars-like yardang swarms, sulfate-bearing salt crusts, strong UV and cold winters — China's flagship published Mars analog (Mars Yard China terrain candidates).
notes.breakdown: Pressure ~70% of sea level (still 40× Mars), winter snow events.
notes.studies: Qaidam-as-Mars-analog papers (Qi et al.); Mars Yard China site selection reports.

notes.why: Tallest fixed megadunes on Earth (up to 480 m) between hypersaline lakes — the height-scale analog for Mars megadunes and for dune-groundwater interaction studies.
notes.breakdown: Dunes are stabilized by moisture; Mars dunes are active under low pressure.
notes.studies: Badain Jaran dune height/aerodynamics studies vs Mars megadune scaling.

notes.why: China's hottest recorded spot, third-lowest land point on Earth (-154 m), hyperarid with saline soils — thermal-extreme plus aridity analog for low-elevation martian basins.
notes.breakdown: Summer monsoon dust events and Earth-scale pressure.
notes.studies: Turpan heat/humidity extremes; saline soil astrobiology tests.

notes.why: A 337,000 km² shifting-sand sea that is one of Earth's great dust-storm engines — process analog for regional dust lifting and storm propagation studied via satellite (MODIS/CALIPSO) for Mars dust climatology comparisons.
notes.breakdown: Dust-weather coupling with water cycle; Mars storms are thermally driven.
notes.studies: Taklamakan dust transport studies; Mars dust-cycle comparative remote sensing.

notes.why: ISRO's recognized Mars-analog zone: a 4.4 km cold desert with permafrost, geothermal sulfur/borax springs, hypersaline Tso Kar lake and intense UV — where Indian Mars-rover prototypes and spacesuits have been field-tested.
notes.breakdown: Oxygen availability and pressure ~60% of sea level; liquid water persists at springs.
notes.studies: ISRO Mars analog trials in Ladakh; Puga geothermal microbiology studies.

notes.why: The ONLY well-preserved terrestrial impact crater excavated in continental flood basalt (Deccan traps) — the closest thing Earth has to lunar/martian craters formed in basaltic crust, with a hypersaline-alkaline lake inside (ISRO lunar analog studies).
notes.breakdown: Lake and lush rim vegetation; 1.8 km scale vs 10-100 km lunar craters.
notes.studies: ISRO Lonar lunar-analog campaigns; Lonar impactite and shock-barometry literature.

notes.why: A >500,000 km² continental flood-basalt province of stacked lava flows — a step-terrain analog for lunar mare basalt plains and Mars flood-lava provinces, far less visited than Iceland.
notes.breakdown: Monsoon weathering and vegetation mask fresh basalt textures.
notes.studies: Deccan lava stratigraphy; mare basalt comparative petrology.

notes.why: A 5.5-million-year sealed cave where ~50 species survive entirely on chemosynthetic bacteria (sulfide/H2 energy) — the best terrestrial model for a subsurface chemolithotrophic biosphere sheltered from surface conditions.
notes.breakdown: Karst cave; biology is carbon-based Earth life, not independent abiogenesis.
notes.studies: Movile Cave microbiology (Sarbu et al. 1994-2020); planetary subsurface habitability reviews.

notes.why: The largest continental flood-basalt province on Earth (1.7 Mkm²): stair-stepped basalt plateaus cut by 800 m canyon systems under continuous permafrost — analog for mare-style lava plains and the walls of martian outflow channels.
notes.breakdown: Heavy snow cover half the year; taiga on lower plateaus.
notes.studies: Siberian Traps volcanology; outflow-channel wall stratigraphy comparisons.

notes.why: The 1975-76 Great Fissure Eruption produced fresh basalt plains, lava tubes and ash 'dead zones' used by the Soviet/Russian planetary program as Moon/Mars field analogs — exceptionally fresh mare-like basalt textures.
notes.breakdown: Active degassing and regional seismicity.
notes.studies: Tolbachik 1975-76 analog studies; basalt texture remote-sensing calibration.

notes.why: High-Arctic continuous permafrost with ice-wedge polygons, pingos and rock glaciers — ESA AMASE's Mars analog for mid-latitude polygonal patterned ground and subsurface ice prospecting.
notes.breakdown: Ocean-moderated climate; ice is at 0°C, not tens-of-kelvin deep cryosphere.
notes.studies: ESA AMASE campaigns (2003-2010); Mars polygonal-terrain analog studies.

notes.why: The canonical cold polar desert: no glaciers in the valleys, salt-encrusted permafrost soils, ephemeral streams — NASA's benchmark Mars analog for cryospheric weathering and life at its limits (kept here as the calibration site to compare newer candidates against).
notes.breakdown: Earth-normal atmosphere/oxygen; summer meltwater pulses.
notes.studies: McKay/Friedmann microbial-permafrost studies; decades of Mars analog benchmarking.

notes.why: Blue-ice ablation zones that concentrate meteorites (including lunar and martian samples like ALH84001 found in similar fields) — the operational analog for planetary sample-recovery expeditions and cryogenic sample preservation.
notes.breakdown: Not a landform analog at all — it is a logistics/sampling-process analog for returned-sample handling.
notes.studies: ANSMET/Frontier Mountain meteorite programs (Folco, Delisle).

notes.why: A 23 km, 39 Ma impact crater in a polar desert — combining impact geology (breccia, shocked gullies) with permafrost conditions; home of NASA's Haughton-Mars Project and FMARS habitat simulations (kept as benchmark).
notes.breakdown: Arctic summer light cycle; carbonate basement.
notes.studies: NASA Haughton-Mars Project (Lee, McKay); Mars Society FMARS missions.

notes.why: The world's best-exposed slice of oceanic crust and mantle: olivine-rich peridotites, serpentinization springs (pH ~11) and hydrothermal altered basalt — NASA/ESA test Mars drills here because it reproduces olivine-bearing crust and subsurface H2-driven habitability.
notes.breakdown: Vegetated wadis nearby; oceanic lithosphere emplacement has no Mars analog.
notes.studies: OmanDrill project; NASA Mars 2020 drill/analog testing; Mars olivine-crust analog papers.

notes.why: Complete ophiolite sequence with classic pillow lavas, sheeted dikes and serpentinized mantle — the model for martian crust stratigraphy interpretations and for hydrogen-driven subsurface microbial ecosystems.
notes.breakdown: Mediterranean climate; sulfide mine tailings dominate parts of the massif.
notes.studies: Troodos serpentinization/H2 microbiology studies; Mars crust stratigraphy analog work.

notes.why: Apollo-era training caldera (NASA geologists 1965-67) with fresh basalt flows, a volcanic collapse lake (Öskjuvatn) and the explosive Víti crater — a compact volcanic-terrain analog for mare volcanology training.
notes.breakdown: Active hydrothermal lake; Iceland's wet climate.
notes.studies: Apollo Iceland field training (1965-67); planetary lava-flow analog studies.

notes.why: One of Earth's largest accessible lava tubes (1.6 km surveyed sections) with intact roofs, collapse skylights and flow ledges — interior-microenvironment analog for lunar rille tubes and Mars skylight habitats.
notes.breakdown: Glacial meltwater ingress; ice formations inside the tube.
notes.studies: Icelandic lava tube surveys; planetary lava-tube habitat studies (Horvath, Boston).

sites.name: Craters of the Moon lava field

notes.why: A 1,600 km² young basalt plain with 60 km of mapped lava tubes, spatter cones and pressure ridges — the NASA-selected Apollo-era analog (Apollo 16/17 geologists trained here) for mare-plains field operations.
notes.breakdown: Rim vegetation (limber pine) recolonizing older flows.
notes.studies: NASA Apollo-era Idaho training (1969); modern cave/robotics analog studies.

notes.why: Apollo 17's official training crater: a 2 km maar ringed by basalt with mantle xenoliths (olivine-rich peridotite nodules) in the rim — crater-exploration EVA training plus direct access to mantle olivine like the olivine seen on Mars.
notes.breakdown: Phreatomagmatic origin (not impact); Chihuahuan scrub vegetation.
notes.studies: Apollo 17 Kilbourne Hole training (Schmitt); Potrillo field Mars analog studies.

notes.why: The freshest large terrestrial impact crater (1.2 km, 50 ka) with exposed rim uplift, inverted ejecta and drill-verified subsurface structure — THE benchmark for fresh simple-crater morphology and Apollo 15/16/17 field geology training.
notes.breakdown: Sedimentary target rock; 50 ka weathering vs millions of years of martian degradation.
notes.studies: Shoemaker 1960s crater studies; Apollo crew training (1967-71); Barringer ejecta research.

notes.why: The world's largest gypsum dune field — bright, high-albedo, salt-rich granular terrain analogous to Mars's bright sulfate/evaporite dune surfaces, plus an active dust-devil observation area.
notes.breakdown: Gypsum chemistry is rare on Mars (sulfates are there, but not as dune sand).
notes.studies: White Sands dust-devil/dune studies; bright-dune spectrometry analog work.

notes.why: A 700 m volcanic maar in the hottest place on Earth (nearby Furnace Creek holds the 56.7 °C world record) with salt pans and scoured badlands — thermal-extreme + crater-morphology combination analog.
notes.breakdown: Maar genesis is volcanic; record heat is solar-driven.
notes.studies: Death Valley geomorphology; heat-extreme instrument testing campaigns.

notes.why: A 7,000 km² endorheic salt chott with polygonal crusts, mirage-shimmering surface and dust lifting — evaporite-basin analog used in planetary surface comparative studies.
notes.breakdown: Winter brine floods; anthropogenic roads cross the pan.
notes.studies: Chott evaporite geochemistry; Mars/Titan evaporite analog discussions.
